warmup.q: data class Batch(val id: String, val paymentIds: List<String>). You build Batch("b-7", ids) from a MutableList holding p1, and later the caller runs ids += "p2". What does batch.paymentIds show?
options: [p1, p2], because the batch holds the same list
It doesn't compile: a MutableList can't be passed as a List
warmup.why: val only stops the property from pointing at another list, and List only stops writes made through that reference. The batch and the caller hold the same ArrayList, so the caller's change shows up in the batch. A MutableList is a List, so passing it compiles. Copy at the boundary (ids.toList()) to take a snapshot.

sections.h: Read-only is not immutable: what val and List really promise
sections.html:
A payout batch is built from a Kafka consumer's buffer, written to a payout file, and then the consumer clears the buffer for the next poll:

Java
record Batch(String id, List<String> paymentIds) {}

Batch batch = new Batch("b-7", buffer);   // buffer is the consumer's ArrayList
payoutFile.write(batch);
buffer.clear();                           // batch.paymentIds() is now empty too
Kotlin
data class Batch(val id: String, val paymentIds: List<String>)

val batch = Batch("b-7", buffer)      // buffer is the consumer's MutableList
payoutFile.write(batch)
buffer.clear()                        // batch.paymentIds is now empty too

Everything in Batch looks frozen: a data class, val properties, a read-only List. But val only means the property can't point at a different list. List only means you can't call add through that reference. Neither freezes the object behind them, and here both sides hold the same ArrayList. The Kotlin docs say it plainly: a read-only interface "prevents accidental modification through that interface. By contrast, an immutable collection doesn't allow you to change its elements after creation."

The read-only part is checked only at compile time. On the JVM, listOf("p1", "p2") is a java.util.Arrays$ArrayList; cast it to MutableList and set(0, "p9") works, while add throws UnsupportedOperationException.

Data classes add two traps of their own. copy() is shallow: "it doesn't copy components recursively". a.copy(id = "p2") shares a's tag list, so a tag added through the copy shows up in the original. And equals compares every property with its own equals, which for BigDecimal includes the scale. Fee("m-1", BigDecimal("10.00")) == Fee("m-1", BigDecimal("10.0")) is false, although compareTo says the amounts are equal. Parse 10.0 from one partner's JSON and compute 10.00 yourself, and your duplicate check misses a real duplicate:

Java
BigDecimal amount = new BigDecimal(json.amount()).setScale(2, RoundingMode.UNNECESSARY);   // same fix
Kotlin
val amount = BigDecimal(json.amount).setScale(2, RoundingMode.UNNECESSARY)   // one scale for all money

UNNECESSARY throws if rounding would be needed, so a third decimal fails loudly instead of being rounded away. Storing money as a Long of cents avoids the question entirely.

So an immutable value needs three layers. Its properties are val. Their types are immutable all the way down: String, BigDecimal, LocalDate, other immutable data classes, immutable collections. And nothing mutable leaks in or out, which at a boundary means a copy: toList() for a snapshot, or toImmutableList() from the next section when you want the type to promise it.

BigDecimal.equals compares the scale too, and data class equals uses it println("5. Fee(10.00) == Fee(10.0): ${Fee("m-1", BigDecimal("10.00")) == Fee("m-1", BigDecimal("10.0"))}") println(" compareTo says equal: ${BigDecimal("10.00").compareTo(BigDecimal("10.0")) == 0}") }

alt.html: package workbench.functional.l08; import java.math.BigDecimal; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.Collections; import java.util.List; /** The same traps in Java: views that change, shallow records, and BigDecimal.equals. */ public class ReadOnlyJava { record Batch(String id, List<String> paymentIds) {} record Fee(String merchantId, BigDecimal amount) {} public static void main(String[] args) { // 1. a record holding the caller's list sees every later change List<String> backing = new ArrayList<>(List.of("p1")); Batch batch = new Batch("b-7", backing); backing.add("p2"); System.out.println("1. batch after the caller adds p2: " + batch.paymentIds()); // 2. Collections.unmodifiableList is a view too: it blocks writes through it, not changes behind it List<String> view = Collections.unmodifiableList(backing); backing.add("p3"); System.out.println("2. unmodifiable view: " + view); // 3. List.copyOf takes a real snapshot (JDK 10+) and rejects writes Batch safe = new Batch("b-8", List.copyOf(backing)); backing.add("p4"); System.out.println("3. snapshot after another add: " + safe.paymentIds()); try { safe.paymentIds().add("p5"); } catch (UnsupportedOperationException e) { System.out.println(" add: UnsupportedOperationException"); } // 4. BigDecimal.equals compares the scale, and record equals uses it System.out.println("4. Fee(10.00).equals(Fee(10.0)): " + new Fee("m-1", new BigDecimal("10.00")).equals(new Fee("m-1", new BigDecimal("10.0")))); System.out.println(" compareTo says equal: " + (new BigDecimal("10.00").compareTo(new BigDecimal("10.0")) == 0)); } }

try.expect: Line 1 shows [p1, p2]: the batch sees the caller's add. Line 2 shows [p1, p2, p3]: a cast gets past the read-only type. listOf is a java.util.Arrays$ArrayList, so set works and add throws. copy() shares the tag list (same list: true), and Fee(10.00) == Fee(10.0) is false while compareTo says equal. Java's Collections.unmodifiableList is also only a view, but List.copyOf is a snapshot. With toList(), line 1 shows [p1]: the batch has its own snapshot. Line 2 now throws UnsupportedOperationException, but only by luck: for one element, toList() returns java.util.Collections$SingletonList. From two elements up it returns a plain ArrayList, and the cast-and-add would work. The read-only type is the only promise you get.

sections.h: Persistent collections: change means a new version
sections.html:
Immutable values pay you back in three ways. You can share them between threads with no lock, because nobody can write ("Don't share: immutability, confinement, ThreadLocal" in the first track). You can keep the old version for an audit trail. And a test can hold the "before" and "after" side by side. The price is that every change makes a new value. Copying a whole ledger to append one entry is what Java does in the Try it, and it costs time and memory in proportion to the list's size, on every change.

Persistent collections avoid most of that copy. A new version shares most of its internal structure with the old one, so adding an entry builds a few new nodes and reuses the rest. The library is kotlinx-collections-immutable, version 0.5.2 in the lab. Its README still says "the library is experimental and the API is subject to change", so treat it as a pre-1.0 dependency. ImmutableList promises that nobody can change the list; PersistentList adds the operations that return a new version:

Java
// Java equivalent: no persistent collections in the JDK, so copy the whole list per version
List<String> v1 = List.of("opening");
List<String> v2 = Stream.concat(v1.stream(), Stream.of("payout:m-acme")).toList();
List<String> tmp = new ArrayList<>(v2);
tmp.addAll(List.of("fee-income", "payout:m-globex"));
List<String> v3 = List.copyOf(tmp);
Kotlin
val v1 = persistentListOf("opening")
val v2 = v1.adding("payout:m-acme")                  // a new list; v1 is untouched
val v3 = v2.addingAll(listOf("fee-income", "payout:m-globex"))
val v4 = v3.mutate { it.removeAt(0); it += "closing" }   // several changes in one go

Notice the names. Until 0.5.0 these methods were called add, remove, put and set, like the mutating methods on MutableList. That invited a quiet bug: ledger.entries.add(entry) as a statement builds a new list and throws it away, and the ledger never changes. Version 0.5.0 renamed the copy-returning methods to adding, removing, putting, replacingAt and removingAt, following a naming proposal (KEEP-0459, still a draft) where a verb like add changes the object and a participle like adding returns a copy, as sorted() does next to sort(). The old names still compile, with a warning: 'fun add(element: Long): PersistentList<Long>' is deprecated. Use adding() instead.

In the lab, the ledger is a data class around a PersistentList<Entry>, and posting returns a new ledger with copy(entries = entries.addingAll(...)). The ledger you posted to is still there, unchanged, for the test to compare against.

alt.html: package workbench.functional.l08; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; /** * Java equivalent: the JDK has no persistent collections. A new version means copying the old one * (O(n) per change) into an unmodifiable list. Structure sharing needs a library. */ public class PersistentJava { static List<String> adding(List<String> list, String element) { List<String> copy = new ArrayList<>(list); // copies every element copy.add(element); return List.copyOf(copy); } public static void main(String[] args) { List<String> v1 = List.of("opening"); List<String> v2 = adding(v1, "payout:m-acme"); List<String> v3 = adding(adding(v2, "fee-income"), "payout:m-globex"); System.out.println("v1 = " + v1); System.out.println("v2 = " + v2); System.out.println("v3 = " + v3); List<String> builder = new ArrayList<>(v3); // several changes: copy once, change, freeze builder.remove(0); builder.add("closing"); List<String> v4 = List.copyOf(builder); System.out.println("v4 = " + v4); System.out.println("v3 = " + v3 + " (unchanged)"); } }

sections.h: Recursion: tailrec is a loop, everything else uses the stack
sections.html:
Functional code often recurses where Java code loops. On the JVM that has a hard limit: every call takes a stack frame, and the JVM never removes a call, even the last call in a method. Sum the numbers 1 to 1,000,000 by recursion and you get a StackOverflowError, in both languages. In Java it overflows even when the recursive call is the last thing the method does.

Kotlin's tailrec moves the fix into the compiler. "When a function is marked with the tailrec modifier and meets the required formal conditions, the compiler optimizes out the recursion, leaving behind a fast and efficient loop based version instead." The trick is an accumulator: make the pending work an argument, so the recursive call is the last thing that happens.

Java
// Java has no tailrec: write the loop the Kotlin compiler would write
static long sumTo(long n) {
    long acc = 0;
    while (n > 0) { acc += n; n--; }
    return acc;
}
Kotlin
tailrec fun sumTo(n: Long, acc: Long = 0): Long = if (n == 0L) acc else sumTo(n - 1, acc + n)
// sumTo(1_000_000) == 500000500000, no stack growth

javap -c shows what the compiler did: sumTo stores the new values into its own parameter slots and ends with goto 0, a jump back to its first instruction. There is no invokestatic sumTo left. The conditions are strict. The function must call itself as its very last operation, not inside try, catch or finally, and it can't be open. Get it wrong and Kotlin only warns: A function is marked as tail-recursive but no tail calls are found. and Recursive call is not a tail call. The code compiles to ordinary recursion and still overflows. Read the warnings.

Some recursion has no tail form. Counting the nodes of a deep tree, such as a merchant hierarchy, makes several recursive calls per node. DeepRecursiveFunction from the standard library runs such a function with its "stack" on the heap, using coroutine machinery. In the Try it it counts a tree 100,001 levels deep, where the same code as a plain function overflows.

Most of the time you need neither. Summing a ledger or applying events to a state is a fold or a sumOf (the collections lesson), which says what it means in one line and compiles to the same kind of loop. Recursion that walks a list with first() and drop(1) is worse than either: drop(1) copies the rest of the list at every step. Keep tailrec for algorithms that are recursive by nature, like walking a chain of refunds back to the original payment.

try.title: Watch tailrec become a goto
steps: Run Recursion.kt. Predict which lines print a number and which print StackOverflowError.
From labs/, run javap -c -p -cp functional/build/classes/kotlin/demo workbench.functional.l08.RecursionKt and find sumTo and sumNaive. Which one calls itself?
Add tailrec in front of fun sumNaive and run again. Read the warnings in the build output.
Run RecursionJava.java. Does sumTail, with its call in tail position, survive?

code.title: Recursion.kt
code.html: package workbench.functional.l08 /** Sums 1..n with recursion that is NOT in tail position: one stack frame per number. */ fun sumNaive(n: Long): Long = if (n == 0L) 0 else n + sumNaive(n - 1) /** The same sum with an accumulator: the recursive call is the last thing it does. */ tailrec fun sumTo(n: Long, acc: Long = 0): Long = if (n == 0L) acc else sumTo(n - 1, acc + n) /** A refund of a refund of a refund: walk back to the original payment. */ data class Txn(val id: String, val parentId: String?) tailrec fun originOf(id: String, byId: Map<String, Txn>): String { val parent = byId.getValue(id).parentId ?: return id return originOf(parent, byId) } /** A merchant hierarchy: counting the nodes is recursion that can't be put in tail form. */ class Node(val children: List<Node>) val countNodes = DeepRecursiveFunction<Node, Long> { node -> var total = 1L for (child in node.children) total += callRecursive(child) // the "stack" lives on the heap total } fun main() { println("tailrec sumTo(1,000,000) = ${sumTo(1_000_000)}") try { println("sumNaive(1,000,000) = ${sumNaive(1_000_000)}") } catch (e: StackOverflowError) { println("sumNaive(1,000,000): StackOverflowError") } println("fold over 1..1,000,000 = ${(1L..1_000_000L).fold(0L) { acc, n -> acc + n }}") val chain = (1..100_000).associate { i -> "t$i" to Txn("t$i", if (i == 1) null else "t${i - 1}") } println("origin of t100000 = ${originOf("t100000", chain)}") var deep = Node(emptyList()) repeat(100_000) { deep = Node(listOf(deep)) } println("nodes in a tree 100,001 levels deep = ${countNodes(deep)}") }

alt.title: RecursionJava.java
alt.html: package workbench.functional.l08; import java.util.stream.LongStream; /** Java has no tailrec, and the JVM doesn't remove tail calls: a call in tail position still uses a frame. */ public class RecursionJava { static long sumNaive(long n) { return n == 0 ? 0 : n + sumNaive(n - 1); } static long sumTail(long n, long acc) { return n == 0 ? acc : sumTail(n - 1, acc + n); } // tail position, still a call static long sumLoop(long n) { // what tailrec writes for you long acc = 0; while (n > 0) { acc += n; n--; } return acc; } public static void main(String[] args) { try { System.out.println("sumTail(1,000,000) = " + sumTail(1_000_000, 0)); } catch (StackOverflowError e) { System.out.println("sumTail(1,000,000): StackOverflowError"); } try { System.out.println("sumNaive(1,000,000) = " + sumNaive(1_000_000)); } catch (StackOverflowError e) { System.out.println("sumNaive(1,000,000): StackOverflowError"); } System.out.println("loop = " + sumLoop(1_000_000)); System.out.println("LongStream.sum = " + LongStream.rangeClosed(1, 1_000_000).sum()); } }

try.expect: sumTo and fold both print 500000500000; sumNaive overflows; originOf walks 100,000 refunds back to t1; countNodes returns 100001. In javap, sumTo ends with goto 0 and never calls itself, while sumNaive has invokestatic sumNaive. Marking sumNaive as tailrec gives A function is marked as tail-recursive but no tail calls are found. and Recursive call is not a tail call., and it still overflows. In Java, sumTail overflows too: the JVM doesn't remove tail calls, so only a loop helps.

sections.h: A functional core decides, a thin shell does the I/O
sections.html:
Here is the track's last step: put the pieces into one shape. The lab's LegacySettlementJob is a real-looking settlement job. In one loop it reads the clock, loads payments, skips refunds, holds payments that are too recent, sums per merchant, computes fees, calls the payout API, posts to the ledger and saves it, with println in between. It works. But to test one fee rule you need a fake store, a fake API, a fixed clock, and assertions on what the fakes recorded.

The fix is the shape from the first lesson of this track, usually called functional core, imperative shell. The core is a pure function. It takes plain values, today's date included, and returns a value that describes what should happen:

Java
static SettlementPlan planSettlement(List<Payment> payments, Map<String, Merchant> merchants, LocalDate today)
Kotlin
fun planSettlement(payments: List<Payment>, merchants: Map<String, Merchant>, today: LocalDate): SettlementPlan

Everything from this track fits in there. filterNot, partition, groupBy and sumOf from the collections lesson do the work. Data classes of vals with BigDecimal at scale 2 carry it. Expected outcomes, like a payment whose merchant we don't know, come back as values in the plan instead of exceptions or log lines (the errors lesson).

The shell is the only code that touches the world, and it has almost no branches:

Java
SettlementPlan run() {
    LocalDate today = LocalDate.now(clock);                                              // 1. read
    SettlementPlan plan = planSettlement(store.capturedPayments(), store.merchants(), today);  // 2. decide
    plan.payouts().forEach(payouts::send);                                               // 3. act
    store.saveLedger(posting(store.loadLedger(), plan.payouts(), "settlement-" + today));
    return plan;
}
Kotlin
fun run(): SettlementPlan {
    val today = LocalDate.now(clock)                                              // 1. read
    val plan = planSettlement(store.capturedPayments(), store.merchants(), today)  // 2. decide
    plan.payouts.forEach(payouts::send)                                           // 3. act
    store.saveLedger(store.loadLedger().posting(plan.payouts, "settlement-$today"))
    return plan
}

The tests change shape with the code. The core gets many small tests that build a list, call a function and compare the result with equals: no fakes, no clock, milliseconds each. Because the date is a parameter, "a payment captured yesterday is held" and "the same payment is paid out next week" are two lines. The shell gets one test with fakes that checks the wiring.

The shell isn't pure and doesn't try to be. The program still does all its I/O. What moved is the decisions: each one now lives where you can test it with a value.

try.title: Run a core and its shell
steps: Read CoreShell.kt. decideVoids is the core and VoidJob is the shell. Predict the two decisions and the one gateway call.
Change now to one day later. Without running anything, which decision changes? Then run it to check.

code.title: CoreShell.kt
code.html: package workbench.functional.l08 import java.time.Clock import java.time.Duration import java.time.Instant import java.time.ZoneOffset data class PendingAuth(val id: String, val amountMinor: Long, val authorizedAt: Instant) sealed interface VoidDecision { data class VoidIt(val authId: String) : VoidDecision data class Keep(val authId: String, val expiresIn: Duration) : VoidDecision } val AUTH_LIFETIME: Duration = Duration.ofDays(7) /** The core: authorizations older than seven days are voided. Pure: the time is a parameter. */ fun decideVoids(auths: List<PendingAuth>, now: Instant): List<VoidDecision> = auths.map { a -> val age = Duration.between(a.authorizedAt, now) if (age >= AUTH_LIFETIME) VoidDecision.VoidIt(a.id) else VoidDecision.Keep(a.id, AUTH_LIFETIME - age) } /** The shell: reads, calls the core, carries out the decisions. No rules in here. */ class VoidJob(private val load: () -> List<PendingAuth>, private val voidAuth: (String) -> Unit, private val clock: Clock) { fun run() { val decisions = decideVoids(load(), clock.instant()) // read, then decide decisions.filterIsInstance<VoidDecision.VoidIt>().forEach { voidAuth(it.authId) } // act } } fun main() { val now = Instant.parse("2026-03-10T09:00:00Z") val auths = listOf( PendingAuth("a1", 1_999, now.minus(Duration.ofDays(8))), PendingAuth("a2", 4_250, now.minus(Duration.ofHours(30))), ) println("core, called with plain values:") decideVoids(auths, now).forEach { println(" $it") } println("shell, with a fixed clock and a fake gateway:") VoidJob({ auths }, { println(" POST /authorizations/$it/void") }, Clock.fixed(now, ZoneOffset.UTC)).run() }

alt.title: CoreShellJava.java
alt.html: package workbench.functional.l08; import java.time.Clock; import java.time.Duration; import java.time.Instant; import java.time.ZoneOffset; import java.util.List; import java.util.function.Consumer; import java.util.function.Supplier; /** The same core and shell in Java: records for the values, a static method for the pure core. */ public class CoreShellJava { record PendingAuth(String id, long amountMinor, Instant authorizedAt) {} sealed interface VoidDecision {} record VoidIt(String authId) implements VoidDecision {} record Keep(String authId, Duration expiresIn) implements VoidDecision {} static final Duration AUTH_LIFETIME = Duration.ofDays(7); /** The core: authorizations older than seven days are voided. Pure: the time is a parameter. */ static List<VoidDecision> decideVoids(List<PendingAuth> auths, Instant now) { return auths.stream().<VoidDecision>map(a -> { Duration age = Duration.between(a.authorizedAt(), now); return age.compareTo(AUTH_LIFETIME) >= 0 ? new VoidIt(a.id()) : new Keep(a.id(), AUTH_LIFETIME.minus(age)); }).toList(); } /** The shell: reads, calls the core, carries out the decisions. */ record VoidJob(Supplier<List<PendingAuth>> load, Consumer<String> voidAuth, Clock clock) { void run() { for (VoidDecision d : decideVoids(load.get(), clock.instant())) { if (d instanceof VoidIt v) voidAuth.accept(v.authId()); } } } public static void main(String[] args) { Instant now = Instant.parse("2026-03-10T09:00:00Z"); List<PendingAuth> auths = List.of( new PendingAuth("a1", 1_999, now.minus(Duration.ofDays(8))), new PendingAuth("a2", 4_250, now.minus(Duration.ofHours(30)))); System.out.println("core, called with plain values:"); decideVoids(auths, now).forEach(d -> System.out.println(" " + d)); System.out.println("shell, with a fixed clock and a fake gateway:"); new VoidJob(() -> auths, id -> System.out.println(" POST /authorizations/" + id + "/void"), Clock.fixed(now, ZoneOffset.UTC)).run(); } }

try.expect: The core prints VoidIt(authId=a1) (8 days old) and Keep(authId=a2, expiresIn=PT138H) (30 hours old, 138 hours left). The shell makes one call, POST /authorizations/a1/void. One day later, a2 is still kept with PT114H left, and a1 is voided as before. You could check that from the core alone, with no clock and no gateway, which is the point.

analogy: A functional core is an accountant who works only from the documents on her desk. You hand her the statements, the fee schedule and today's date, and she hands back a written plan: pay these merchants these amounts, hold these payments. She never phones the bank or looks at the wall clock. The imperative shell is the office manager who fetches the documents and then makes the phone calls the plan lists. To check the accountant, you give her a sample pile of papers and read her plan, with no phone lines needed. The analogy breaks in one place: a real accountant would notice if the pile of papers changed while she was reading. Code doesn't, which is why the documents you hand the core must be immutable.
world: Most payments services already have the shell. It is the Quarkus resource, the Kafka consumer, the scheduled job, the Temporal activity. What's usually missing is the pure core underneath. A Temporal workflow makes the split explicit, because workflow code must be deterministic and all I/O goes into activities, so the decision logic in a workflow is already a core in disguise. Look for methods that call Instant.now(), LocalDate.now() or UUID.randomUUID() in the middle of business rules, and pass those values in instead. Look for data classes that hold a MutableList from a caller, and copy at the boundary. And check every BigDecimal you put in a data class: normalize the scale when you parse, or two equal payments from two acquirers won't be equal.
mistake: The most common mistake is believing a data class of vals is immutable, and so safe to share, cache or use as a map key, while one of its properties is a list the caller still holds. People make it because everything they can see says "frozen": data class, val, List. But a read-only List is a view, and the class holds the caller's object. The batch changes when the caller's buffer changes, a cached value changes after it was cached, and a key changes its hashCode while it sits in a HashMap. The fix is to copy at the boundary: Batch(id, ids.toList()), or better, make the property an ImmutableList or PersistentList and convert with toImmutableList(), so the type says what you mean.

compare.title: Immutable values and a pure core: Java records vs Kotlin data classes

java.title: Settlement.java
java.html: record Payout(String merchantId, BigDecimal gross, BigDecimal fee, BigDecimal net) {} record Ledger(List<Entry> entries) { Ledger { entries = List.copyOf(entries); } // snapshot: nobody can change it later Ledger posting(List<Entry> more) { // a new version, by copying everything List<Entry> all = new ArrayList<>(entries); all.addAll(more); return new Ledger(all); } } static BigDecimal fee(BigDecimal gross, BigDecimal rate) { // pure: same inputs, same output return gross.multiply(rate).setScale(2, RoundingMode.HALF_EVEN); }

kotlin.title: Settlement.kt
kotlin.html: data class Payout(val merchantId: String, val gross: BigDecimal, val fee: BigDecimal, val net: BigDecimal) data class Ledger(val entries: PersistentList<Entry>) // the type promises it can't change fun Ledger.posting(more: List<Entry>): Ledger = copy(entries = entries.addingAll(more)) // a new version that shares structure fun fee(gross: BigDecimal, rate: BigDecimal): BigDecimal = // pure: same inputs, same output (gross * rate).setScale(2, RoundingMode.HALF_EVEN)

compare.note: Both languages give you a value type with structural equality, and in both equals uses BigDecimal.equals, so the scale counts. Kotlin's data class adds copy(), which Java records lack (you write "withers" by hand), and both are shallow. The real difference is in collections. Java's List.copyOf makes a runtime-unmodifiable snapshot but every new version copies the whole list. Kotlin's List is only a compile-time read-only view, so you need toList() for a snapshot or kotlinx.collections.immutable for a real guarantee; its PersistentList makes new versions cheaply by sharing structure. The pure functions themselves look the same in both languages. Purity is a habit, not a keyword: neither compiler checks it.

worked.title: Pull the decisions out of a chargeback job

steps.say: A nightly job handles open chargebacks: escalate a case whose deadline is two days away or less, accept the loss once the deadline has passed, otherwise wait. Before reading on, label every line as read, decide or act.
steps.code: fun runChargebacks() { for (case in repo.openCases()) { // read val daysLeft = ChronoUnit.DAYS.between(LocalDate.now(), case.deadline) // read (the clock!) if (daysLeft < 0) { // decide scheme.acceptLoss(case.id) // act repo.close(case.id) // act } else if (daysLeft <= 2 && !case.evidenceSent) { // decide ops.escalate(case.id, "deadline in $daysLeft days") // act } } }

alt.html: void runChargebacks() { for (Case c : repo.openCases()) { // read long daysLeft = ChronoUnit.DAYS.between(LocalDate.now(), c.deadline()); // read (the clock!) if (daysLeft < 0) { // decide scheme.acceptLoss(c.id()); // act repo.close(c.id()); // act } else if (daysLeft <= 2 && !c.evidenceSent()) { // decide ops.escalate(c.id(), "deadline in " + daysLeft + " days"); // act } } }

steps.say: 1. Name the decisions as values. A sealed type makes the plan explicit and lets the shell's when be exhaustive.
steps.code: sealed interface CaseAction { data class AcceptLoss(val caseId: String) : CaseAction data class Escalate(val caseId: String, val daysLeft: Long) : CaseAction data class Wait(val caseId: String) : CaseAction }

alt.html: sealed interface CaseAction {} record AcceptLoss(String caseId) implements CaseAction {} record Escalate(String caseId, long daysLeft) implements CaseAction {} record Wait(String caseId) implements CaseAction {}

steps.say: 1. Write the core as a pure function. The clock becomes a parameter, today, and the result is a list of decisions. Every rule is now testable with one line: decide(listOf(case), LocalDate.of(2026, 3, 10)).
steps.code: fun decide(cases: List<Case>, today: LocalDate): List<CaseAction> = cases.map { case -> val daysLeft = ChronoUnit.DAYS.between(today, case.deadline) when { daysLeft < 0 -> CaseAction.AcceptLoss(case.id) daysLeft <= 2 && !case.evidenceSent -> CaseAction.Escalate(case.id, daysLeft) else -> CaseAction.Wait(case.id) } }

alt.html: static List<CaseAction> decide(List<Case> cases, LocalDate today) { return cases.stream().<CaseAction>map(c -> { long daysLeft = ChronoUnit.DAYS.between(today, c.deadline()); if (daysLeft < 0) return new AcceptLoss(c.id()); if (daysLeft <= 2 && !c.evidenceSent()) return new Escalate(c.id(), daysLeft); return new Wait(c.id()); }).toList(); }

steps.say: 1. The shell reads, calls the core and carries out each action with an exhaustive when. It has no rules left, so one test with fakes covers it. The many rule tests go against decide with plain values.
steps.code: fun runChargebacks() { val actions = decide(repo.openCases(), LocalDate.now(clock)) // read, then decide for (action in actions) when (action) { // act is CaseAction.AcceptLoss -> { scheme.acceptLoss(action.caseId); repo.close(action.caseId) } is CaseAction.Escalate -> ops.escalate(action.caseId, "deadline in ${action.daysLeft} days") is CaseAction.Wait -> Unit } }

alt.html: void runChargebacks() { List<CaseAction> actions = decide(repo.openCases(), LocalDate.now(clock)); // read, then decide for (CaseAction action : actions) { // act switch (action) { case AcceptLoss a -> { scheme.acceptLoss(a.caseId()); repo.close(a.caseId()); } case Escalate e -> ops.escalate(e.caseId(), "deadline in " + e.daysLeft() + " days"); case Wait w -> { } } } }

lab.title: Split the settlement job into a pure core and a thin shell
steps: Run the tests. All eight fail. Seven of them call planSettlement or posting with plain values: no fakes and no clock.
Read LegacySettlementJob.run and label each line read, decide or act. Model.kt holds the types and needs no changes.
Write planSettlement in SettlementCore.kt from the rules in its KDoc. today is a parameter; don't touch a clock.
Write SettlementJob.run as a thin shell: read, call the core, send each payout, post and save the ledger once, return the plan.
Run the tests until all eight pass. Then ask: which test would fail if planSettlement called LocalDate.now() instead of using today?
hints: partition splits a list in two in one pass. Use it twice: first known and unknown merchants, then due and held payments.
sumOf { it.amount } has a BigDecimal overload. Round the fee with setScale(2, RoundingMode.HALF_EVEN), or the test's BigDecimal("3.64") won't equal your 3.63950.
groupBy keeps first-seen order. toSortedMap() orders the groups by merchant id.
In the shell, plan.payouts.forEach(payouts::send) and store.loadLedger().posting(plan.payouts, "settlement-$today") cover steps 3 and 4.

drill.title: tailrec from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. Write originOf(id, byId), which follows parentId links from a refund back to the original payment, as a tailrec function. Then write the Java loop. Last, predict: what happens if you add a log.debug(...) line after the recursive call?

answer.html: tailrec fun originOf(id: String, byId: Map<String, Txn>): String { val parent = byId.getValue(id).parentId ?: return id // no parent: this is the original return originOf(parent, byId) // the last thing the function does } // A log line after the call makes it no longer a tail call: Kotlin warns // "Recursive call is not a tail call." and compiles ordinary recursion, which can overflow.

alt.html: static String originOf(String id, Map<String, Txn> byId) { String current = id; while (true) { String parent = byId.get(current).parentId(); if (parent == null) return current; // no parent: this is the original current = parent; // what tailrec's goto does } }

recap: val stops reassignment and List stops writes through that reference. Neither freezes the object: a read-only view changes when its backing list does.
copy() is shallow, and data class equals uses BigDecimal.equals, which compares the scale. Normalize money when you parse it.
kotlinx.collections.immutable 0.5.2, still marked experimental, gives persistent collections: adding, putting and removingAt return new versions that share structure, and mutate { } batches changes.

tailrec turns a self-call in tail position into a goto. Anywhere else it is only a warning, and the stack still overflows. DeepRecursiveFunction handles deep non-tail recursion, and fold is usually simplest.
A functional core decides from plain values, with the clock passed in; a thin shell reads, calls the core and does the I/O.
Core tests need no fakes and no clock; the shell needs one wiring test.

explain.prompt: A new teammate asks why the settlement job was split into planSettlement and SettlementJob, when the old job "worked fine". Explain what changed and how it changes the tests.
explain.answer: The old job worked, but its decisions were mixed with its I/O. It read the clock, loaded data, applied the fee and hold rules, called the payout API and saved the ledger in one loop, so testing a single rule needed a fake store, a fake API and a fixed clock, plus checks on what the fakes recorded. Now planSettlement is a pure function: payments, merchants and today's date go in, and a plan comes out, with the same answer every time. All the rules live there, and each test builds a few values and compares the plan with equals, in milliseconds. A different day is just a different argument. SettlementJob keeps only the I/O: read, call the core, send the payouts, post and save the ledger. It has almost no branches, so one test with fakes is enough to check the wiring. The data is immutable too, so the plan and the ledger versions can't change behind our backs while we test or retry.

deeper.html:
Immutability is also a concurrency tool, and the memory model track explains why. A val property compiles to a final field, and the Java memory model gives final fields a special guarantee: once the constructor has finished, any thread that sees the object sees those fields fully set, without a lock, as long as the constructor didn't let this escape ("Safe publication, final fields and escaping this"). So an object whose state is all vals of immutable types can be handed to another thread with no synchronization at all. A persistent collection extends that: one thread builds a new version with adding while other threads keep reading the old one, and neither can disturb the other. The catch is the same as in the first section. A val holding a MutableList gets the guarantee only for the reference, not for the list's contents.

The naming change in kotlinx.collections.immutable came with a compiler feature. The 0.5.0 line builds the library itself with Kotlin's Experimental return-value checker in its strictest mode, -Xreturn-value-checker=full. The checker arrived in Kotlin 2.3.0, is off by default, and warns when a call's result is ignored. Both changes go after the same bug: a new version computed and then dropped.

On recursion, arrow-core 2.3.0 also contains a MemoizedDeepRecursiveFunction, a memoizing variant of the standard library's DeepRecursiveFunction. Reach for either only after a plain fold or a loop has been ruled out.
